title: Is physiological equivalent temperature (PET) a superior screening tool for heat stress risk than wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) index? Eight years of data from the Gothenburg half marathon
authors: Thorsson S, Rayner D, Palm G, Lindberg F, Carlstrom E, Borjesson M, et al.
population: Gothenburg half marathon 2010-2017 (eight editions): meteorological data and ambulance transport records
findings: PET correlated best with ambulance-required assistance (R2 = 0.72, p = 0.008) and collapses (R2 = 0.71, p = 0.008).
UTCI followed (R2 = 0.64 for both, p = 0.017), whereas WBGT correlated substantially worse (R2 = 0.56, p = 0.031 and p = 0.033).
Compared with PET, WBGT underestimates heat stress, especially at high radiant heat load.
Collapse rate increases with heat stress; a large increase from the day before the race seems to have an impact.
limitations: One race, eight editions (eight data points), medical-incident outcome not performance; PET/UTCI need more inputs and are less standardized for racing; the authors call for further investigation of PET alongside WBGT, not replacement.
implications: Treat WBGT as a screening and pacing index, not a complete safety measure: warn on high solar or radiant load and on a large day-over-day temperature jump.
Keep the heat-index implementation modular so PET or UTCI can be added later; no change to pace-penalty parameters is justified by this study.
